label.rationale: g6 sets a forcing mating attack and Black can delay it only by checks and material offers. The shown alternatives are directed at the same mate.
Rxb6 is needed before the rook attacks c6. Rc1 and the competing pawn majorities also create an independent rook-endgame plan.
Nxe5 and Bg4 lead to a concrete queen exchange; f5 permits en passant and different recaptures. The e-pawn and resulting central structure influence the later play.
Nxe5 leads to a specific Bxa2 and Nxg6 capture sequence. c5 and the different knight setups determine longer-term play with opposite-side kings.
Nf5 uses the e7 fork route and must be compared with the exact exd5 exchange. The d-file rook arrangement is independently important after the bishop trade.
Queenside castling changes the concrete Bxg2 threats and the available exchanges. Both king shelter and pressure from the c-pawn persist through separate choices.
Clearing b4 prevents the advanced pawn from capturing on c3 and changes the a-pawn threat and rook routes. Separate tactical necessity beyond the exchange is uncertain.
Qxf2+ and Ng4+ recover material after Qh6. The white rook's route and Black's advancing centre remain factors in the quieter alternatives.
Both sides manoeuvre around the d6 outpost and queenside pawn exchanges. The close candidates reorganise rooks with no verified decisive tactic separating them.
Kxf7 allows the exact Nxc6 sequence. Independently, the opened d-file gives the rooks an enduring entry after the queen trade.
The checks and exchanges on f7 alter whether e6 wins material. The h-pawn advance and Black's alternative queenside break shape continuing play.
Qc5+ and the rook invasion create concrete material threats. The f-pawn also supplies a separate plan if Black avoids the checking sequence.
Knight rerouting and the central d-pawn break govern the structure. The legal variations show mainly manoeuvring and preparation.
Rxd4+ and the bishop recapture change the rook liquidation. The pressure on the d-file and the queenside passer shape the close replies after Nb7.
Black's b4 lever and deployment of the knight on c4 affect the bishop and a-file play. The checking route to c2 leaves tactical significance uncertain.
Different recaptures on e5 decide whether Qxg5+ is available. The resulting kingside pawn shape and open lines continue to matter.
Rxh5 demands gxh5 before the rook invades with check. The resulting bishop endgame offers separate central and queenside pawn plans.
Rf4 and b5 change the rook trades and the outside passer. The compensation after the exchanges leaves a distinct tactical verdict uncertain.
Nxe4+ and Qxg3+ deflect White's king and force the queen trade, with mating alternatives. Independent strategic relevance is unclear.
White chooses between a queenside pawn advance and central rook coordination. Black's h-pawn and the d2 entry remain strategic constraints.
Switching rooks between the a- and b-files shapes the exchange and control of a6. The close lines revolve around coordination and file control.
The d4 or f6 break changes the centre while White chooses how to coordinate queen and knight. The compared moves do not hinge on an isolated forcing tactic.
The d-file, open c-file and knight routes govern the exchanges. The top continuations are different sensible piece arrangements.
Castling, a5 and h6 change the rook files and the c4 pressure on the knight. The exchanges serve those longer-term plans.
The rook exchanges and knight reroutes aim at control of the centre. f4 and c5 compete as structural breaks.
White can take the bishop or keep the knight and push a7. The distant passers clearly drive the choices, with the independent tactical effect uncertain.
Nc2 makes a direct promotion sequence possible. Black's other passed pawn and the minor pieces' ability to restrict the blockading king determine separate routes.
Qd3 confronts Rh4 and a concrete follow-up against the king; Qd1 chooses a liquidation. The rook and kingside pawn setup affect the longer game.
a5 allows en passant and the concrete queen capture on d6. The central structure and queenside expansion also give independent planning choices.
Bxe5 neutralises the threat and changes the possible queen trades. Black's use of the d-file and the strong knight after exchanges are separate considerations.
Bh2 forces material loss or mate through the g1 threat. The difference between choices follows directly from that attack.
White must calculate the knight and rook captures on d4 after the queen moves. There is an independent f- and g-file coordination problem after the exchanges.
The checks against Black's king lead to exact captures after Kg7. The h-pawn and central pawn breaks give independent plans in the quiet replies.
White must handle the queen's checking resource, including the forced queen trade. The b-pawn advance and the seventh-rank rook are separate plans.
Black can trade off b7 for rook activity and holds different knight placements. The strong knight and queenside pawn structure are the main factors.
Bxc3 changes whether Bxa7 comes first in the exchange. The a-pawn advance and blockade shape the quieter rook play independently.
e4 changes the exact promotion race and can throw away the win. King access to the opposing pawn chain and distant passed pawns are separate strategic constraints.
The e4 break and the coordination of rooks on c and d govern the choices. No concrete decisive tactic distinguishes the leading lines.
Rc3 and Nxc3+ depend on precise calculation before the king goes forward. The d-file pressure and the enduring d-pawn are independent strategic factors.
Nb6+ changes which bishop or knight is captured around the king. White's space and the kingside pawn-lock alternatives persist as an independent factor.
